docs.title: Two-Way Communication & Readiness for Winter Storms
docs.text:
Hoopa Valley Tribe • Columbia NCDP • Tribal Resilience Initiative

The initiative is a: - Co-designing sovereign text simulations for Hoopa Valley and neighboring Tribal Nations. 

- Twilio.org & Open-source tools built with Columbia University, National Center for Disaster Preparedness (NCDP) & Eugene Wu Lab (NSF Grant #2103794).

The project strengthens community readiness before severe winter weather strikes.

docs.title: Foundation & Governance
docs.text:
The project's foundation and governance are built on: - Tribal Data Ownership: ensuring that Tribes maintain full control over data storage, access, and deletion.

- ** Open-Source Codebase**: the platform uses an open-source codebase that is publicly adaptable via columbia-desdr.github.io.

- **Co-Design Team**: Led through a close co-design partnership with Dan Osgood and RobRoy from Hoopa Valley Tribe.

docs.title: Hoopa Valley Facility Network
docs.text:
During an emergency, the system coordinates staging and respite across five key facilities:

Hoopa Facility Location Emergency Staging Role Community Center 11860 State Hwy 96 (Agency) Central Red Cross shelter & supply hub K'ima:w Medical Center 535 Airport Rd Medical triage & critical device power Kim Yerton Library 370 Loop Rd Daytime warming & clean-air respite Hoopa School Gyms Loop Rd / Central Valley High-capacity congregate evacuation Willow Creek 8 miles off territory Alternative option with additional capacity

docs.title: Regional Replication & GitHub Deployment
docs.text: This framework is built to be adapted and self-hosted by neighboring Tribal Nations: - Multi-hazard ready: Customize the SMS scripts for wildfires, floods, or other regional emergencies. - Local landmarks & language: Swap in local road names, shelter locations, and Tribal audio recordings. - Inter-Tribal mutual aid: Share operational lessons across Yurok, Karuk, and neighboring communities. - Self-hosted on GitHub: Fork the open-source codebase and connect your own SMS phone line.

docs.title: Try the Demo & Get Involved
docs.text: Bring two-way SMS readiness exercises to your Nation: - Test live keywords: Text the demo line at +1 (646) 217-0881 - Explore the open code: at columbia-desdr.github.io - Contact the team: Reach out to daniel.osgood@columbia.edu at the National Center for Disaster Preparedness

docs.title: Interactive Exercise: Four SMS Simulations
docs.text:
The interactive exercise uses four coordinated SMS simulations to test live triage, peer-prediction empathy, and shelter staging before winter storms hit:

Step & Keyword Focus Area Function 01 • HVTstorm Storm Memory Paints the picture of past storm impacts at the Hoopa Valley Tribe. 02 • HVTalert Live Crisis Routing Branches rescues, sandbags, and volunteers during an active event. 03 • HVTsafe Discrete Discussions Surfaces unspoken evacuation barriers anonymously. 04 • HVTcoordinate Resource Staging Aligns generators, shelters, and supply hubs.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Community Storm Memory (HVTstorm)
docs.text: This simulation gathers historical storm experiences from both residents and responders to identify real-world case studies and community needs: - Community Experiences: Residents share past challenges—such as unreachable grocery stores, power loss, and missing emergency updates—alongside community support efforts like sharing firewood, shoveling driveways, and checking on neighbors on foot. - Responder Actions & Hazards: Government and Tribal responders document past actions (plowing, sanding roads, clearing trees, opening warming shelters) and recurring hazards like downed power lines, active mudslides, and black ice.

docs.title: Exercise 2: Active Blizzard & Travel Ban (HVTalert)
docs.text:
During an active emergency, HVTalert automates live triage by routing residents based on their immediate situation:

Initial Reply Automated Follow-Up Questions OES Action Output 1. My home is impacted Landmark, headcount, oxygen/wheelchair needs, 4x4 access Priority rescue dispatch list 2. I need resources Specific resources needed, transport access Resource and staging dispatch 3. I have information or resources Wellness check, hazard report, community resource offer Verified situational map or volunteer pool

docs.title: Exercise 3: Safe Space for Challenging Discussions (HVTsafe)
docs.text:
Evacuation decisions are rarely simple. HVTsafe creates an anonymous space for residents to discuss tough household dilemmas—such as leaving animals behind, guarding homes, or caring for Elders. Using peer-mirror scoring, participants guess how their neighbors responded to help break feelings of isolation, while an anonymous community board surfaces practical solutions for Tribal planners.

(Note: Pilot exercise data exploring how household roles shape evacuation willingness is featured in the accompanying presentation charts.)

docs.title: Exercise 4: Three-Track Resource & Shelter Engineering (HVTcoordinate)
docs.text: To align logistics across the entire community, HVTcoordinate runs three simultaneous tracks: - Track 1 (Residents): Maps household valley sectors, medical power dependencies, and endurance limits. - Track 2 (Providers): Audits facility generator fuel supplies and staffing bottlenecks. - Track 3 (Leadership): Evaluates central hub staging versus decentralized sector supply caches.

docs.title: The Communication Shift: From Broadcasting to Listening
docs.text:
Traditional emergency systems rely on one-way alerts that broadcast information without knowing who actually needs help. Our model shifts the focus from broadcasting to listening by using two-way SMS that works even on a weak cell signal:

One-Way Alerts (Traditional) Two-Way SMS (Our Model) Zero feedback: Responders do not know who needs rescue. Live triage: Residents report exact needs quickly. Outside messengers: Generic alerts often face low local trust. Trusted Tribal voice: Uses local landmarks and Tribal protocols. Bandwidth heavy: Web links fail during severe outages. 1-bar resilience: Plain SMS queues and sends without internet. Siloed systems: Tribal and state data remain disconnected. Shared picture: Connects Elders, field crews, and OES.

docs.title: Hoopa Valley Operational Reality
docs.text: Emergency planning in Hoopa Valley must account for steep canyon geography and winter isolation: - Severed travel routes: Landslides and fallen trees frequently block Highway 96 and Bald Hills Road. - Extended power loss: Multi-day PG&E outages threaten home heating and critical medical oxygen devices. - Rural addressing: Many households rely on local landmarks and mile markers rather than standard street addresses. - Sector isolation: The valley's North, Central, and South sectors can easily become cut off from one another during a storm.
